title: What Makes the Human Brain Big

generated.pipeline: extract → Codex draft → Codex accuracy gate + fix (fresh context)

cards.front: Which basic building blocks and arrangement do human and chimpanzee cortices share?
cards.back: The same main cell classes, six cortical layers, and kinds of progenitor.
cards.quote: Yet both are built from the same main classes of cell, arranged in the same six cortical layers, by the same kinds of progenitor.

cards.front: What adult human neuron totals did Azevedo and colleagues report, and what was their sample?
cards.back: About 86 billion neurons overall and 16 billion in cerebral cortex: means from four adult men.
cards.quote: about 86 billion neurons in the adult human brain, about 16 billion of them in the cerebral cortex, the mean from four adult men
cards.section: A bigger sheet, not a thicker one

cards.front: Why describe the human brain as a scaled-up primate brain when discussing neuron number?
cards.back: Its neuron count is about what is predicted for a primate brain of its size; the count is not unusually high for that size.
cards.quote: That is about the number you would predict for a primate brain of its size
cards.section: A bigger sheet, not a thicker one

cards.front: What approximate human-to-mouse cortical thickness and surface-area ratios did Rakic summarize?
cards.back: About twice the thickness and roughly a thousand times the surface area.
cards.quote: The human cortex is only about twice as thick as a mouse's, but its surface area is roughly a thousand times larger
cards.section: A bigger sheet, not a thicker one

cards.front: Model cortex as area × thickness. If one cortex has 1,000 times the area and twice the thickness of another, what is its volume ratio?
cards.back: Volume ratio = 1,000 × 2 = 2,000. Area supplies a factor of 1,000; thickness supplies a factor of 2.
cards.quote: Height gives a factor of 2 and area a factor of about 1,000, and 2 × 1,000 = 2,000.
cards.section: A bigger sheet, not a thicker one

cards.front: Why can repeated progenitor-doubling divisions increase neuron output more than repeated direct asymmetric neurogenic divisions?
cards.back: Doubling creates additional progenitors that keep dividing, so output compounds. Direct asymmetric neurogenic divisions preserve the progenitor pool and add neurons without expanding it.
cards.quote: A division that makes two progenitors adds a progenitor that keeps dividing, so repeated rounds compound
cards.section: A bigger sheet, not a thicker one

cards.front: Two developing tissues end with different neuron totals. Why is the total alone insufficient to establish that one underwent more progenitor-doubling divisions?
cards.back: The division history is not identified by the endpoint. The stated growth rules also allow a longer neurogenic period, altered survival, or altered packing to change totals; distinguish these alternatives before attributing the difference to doubling.
cards.quote: A longer neurogenic period, or changes in how neurons survive or pack, also change the total.
cards.section: A bigger sheet, not a thicker one

cards.front: A symmetric proliferative division makes {{c1::two progenitors}} from one progenitor.
cards.back: If every progenitor divides this way once, the pool doubles.
cards.quote: In a symmetric proliferative division, the doubling division, one progenitor makes two
cards.section: More columns, not a thicker cortex

cards.front: How does a direct asymmetric neurogenic division affect the radial glial pool?
cards.back: It leaves the pool unchanged: each radial glial cell makes one radial glial cell and one neuron.
cards.quote: In an asymmetric neurogenic division, a radial glial cell makes one copy of itself and one neuron
cards.section: More columns, not a thicker cortex

cards.front: What structures together form a radial unit in the radial unit hypothesis?
cards.back: A patch of founder progenitors at the ventricle and the column of neurons it produces.
cards.quote: A radial unit is a patch of founders at the ventricle together with the one column of neurons it makes
cards.section: More columns, not a thicker cortex

cards.front: Under the radial unit hypothesis, how do unit number and neurons per unit affect cortical geometry?
cards.back: More units increase area; more neurons per unit increase thickness, assuming equal surface patches and unchanged neuronal packing.
cards.quote: the number of units sets the area of the cortex, and the number of neurons each unit makes sets its thickness.
cards.section: More columns, not a thicker cortex

cards.front: A fixed-column model starts with 2,000 founders, each making 80 neurons. Add two symmetric founder rounds before neurogenesis. What are the final neuron count and area ratio, with packing unchanged?
cards.back: Founders = 2,000 × 2² = 8,000. Neurons = 8,000 × 80 = 640,000, versus 160,000 initially. Area increases fourfold; thickness stays unchanged.
cards.quote: units after k extra symmetric rounds = starting units × 2ᵏ
cards.section: More columns, not a thicker cortex

cards.front: A fixed-column model has 2,000 units producing 80 neurons each. Instead of expanding founders, add four direct neurogenic divisions per unit. What happens to neuron count and area?
cards.back: Each unit makes 84 neurons. Total = 2,000 × 84 = 168,000, versus 160,000: a 5% increase. Unit number and area stay unchanged; columns become slightly taller.
cards.quote: each extra direct neurogenic division adds one neuron to a unit
cards.section: More columns, not a thicker cortex

cards.front: In a model with equal-sized cortical units and unchanged packing, how many whole extra founder-doubling rounds first reach at least a thousandfold area increase?
cards.back: 2⁹ = 512 and 2¹⁰ = 1,024, so ten rounds first reach the threshold. This is a model calculation, not evidence that those divisions occurred.
cards.quote: With every unit the same size and nothing else changed, ten extra rounds would turn a mouse-sized sheet into a human-sized one.
cards.section: More columns, not a thicker cortex

cards.front: Stabilized β-catenin in mouse neural progenitors increased cycle re-entry, cortical area, and folding. Does this establish the developmental route of primate cortical folding?
cards.back: No. It shows that more founder divisions can enlarge the cortical sheet in mice. The folds arose from an enlarged ventricular surface, unlike primate growth, and the mice did not live past birth.
cards.quote: the experiment shows that more founder divisions can enlarge the sheet, not how it happened in primates.
cards.section: More columns, not a thicker cortex

cards.front: What explained larger human brain organoids in the human–chimpanzee–gorilla comparison by Benito-Kwiecinski and colleagues?
cards.back: Human neuroepithelial cells took longer to become radial glia, giving the founder pool more time to expand. This was an organoid comparison.
cards.quote: which gave the founder pool more time to expand.
cards.section: More columns, not a thicker cortex

cards.front: Why is a radial unit an approximation rather than a strict map of every cortical lineage?
cards.back: Related neurons can spread sideways, and inhibitory interneurons migrate tangentially into cortex. The unit-number–area link remains a working model.
cards.quote: Lineage tracing in rodents and ferrets later found that related neurons can spread sideways
cards.section: More columns, not a thicker cortex

cards.front: In developing cortex, apical points toward the {{c1::ventricle}}, whereas basal points toward the brain surface.
cards.quote: apical means toward the ventricle, basal toward the brain surface.
cards.section: A second place to double

cards.front: What distinguishes direct from indirect neurogenesis by radial glia?
cards.back: Direct neurogenesis makes a neuron straight from radial glia. Indirect neurogenesis goes through an intermediate progenitor that divides to produce neurons.
cards.quote: Making a neuron straight from a radial glial cell is the direct route of neurogenesis, going through an intermediate progenitor the indirect route
cards.section: More columns, not a thicker cortex

cards.front: Where are classic outer radial glia found, and which connection do they retain or lack?
cards.back: In the outer subventricular zone, away from the ventricle. They retain a long basal fibre but lack ventricular contact.
cards.quote: Unlike classical radial glia, they had no process touching the ventricle.
cards.section: A second place to double

cards.front: In live human fetal cortical slices, a daughter of an outer radial glial cell retains its fibre and divides again; another becomes an intermediate progenitor. What capacities do these observations demonstrate?
cards.back: Self-renewal and supply of the indirect neurogenic route away from the ventricle. They do not measure the total neurons such cells contribute in a living fetus.
cards.quote: Daughters followed in the films could inherit the fibre and divide again, or become intermediate progenitors expressing TBR2.
cards.section: A second place to double

cards.front: Why did live imaging of fetal macaque basal radial glia add a second amplification site to the radial unit model?
cards.back: Some divisions left both daughters as progenitors, showing that basal radial glia can double during neurogenesis, away from the ventricular founders.
cards.quote: These cells also made proliferative divisions, in which both daughters stay progenitors.
cards.section: A second place to double

cards.front: A toy lineage starts with one progenitor for 60 rounds. Each progenitor makes two progenitors with probability 0.1, otherwise one progenitor and one neuron. None stops or dies. Find expected total neurons.
cards.back: The expected pool before round r + 1 is 1.1^r. Total neurons = 0.9 × Σ(r=0…59)1.1^r = 9 × (1.1⁶⁰ − 1) ≈ 2,731, versus 60 without doubling.
cards.quote: Nine tenths of the pool make a neuron in each round, which sums to 9 × (1.1⁶⁰ − 1) ≈ 2,731 neurons.
cards.section: A second place to double

cards.front: In a cortical growth cartoon with fixed packing, extra neurons climb straight, parallel fibres into existing columns. What happens to thickness, and how could a divergent scaffold change the outcome?
cards.back: Thickness increases with parallel fibres. Diverging fibres let migrating neurons spread sideways, favouring area growth; actual geometry also depends on neuronal packing and tissue growth.
cards.quote: They fan the radial scaffold outward, so the neurons that climb them can spread sideways.
cards.section: A second place to double

cards.front: DAPT treatment of human fetal cortical slices lowers the SOX2-high fraction and raises the TBR2-high fraction. Why does this support, but not isolate, a role for Notch in maintaining outer radial glia?
cards.back: The shift supports γ-secretase-dependent maintenance of the radial glial state. Notch requires γ-secretase, but DAPT blocks other targets too, so Notch alone is not established as responsible.
cards.quote: Because DAPT blocks other γ-secretase targets too, this points to a role for Notch signalling
cards.section: A second place to double

cards.front: How does outer radial glial abundance vary among primates, ferret, and mouse?
cards.back: They are abundant in primates and ferret but rare in mouse; the human outer subventricular zone is especially large. They are not uniquely human.
cards.quote: The difference is one of degree: these cells are abundant in primates and ferret and rare in mouse
cards.section: A second place to double

cards.front: A marmoset has an outer subventricular zone but a nearly smooth cortex. What does this imply about whether outer radial glia alone produce folds?
cards.back: They are not sufficient on their own. Their presence in a nearly smooth cortex separates having these progenitors from necessarily producing cortical folds.
cards.quote: The marmoset, a monkey with a nearly smooth cortex, also has an outer subventricular zone
cards.section: A second place to double

cards.front: What happened to basal progenitors when ARHGAP11B was introduced into embryonic mouse cortex?
cards.back: The number of basal progenitors increased.
cards.quote: Electroporated into the embryonic mouse cortex, it increased the number of basal progenitors.
cards.section: Genes that only humans have

cards.front: What did ARHGAP11B expression in marmoset fetuses establish about cortical output?
cards.back: It enlarged the neocortex and increased upper-layer neurons, showing that a human-specific gene can expand cortical output in a primate, without establishing human evolutionary causation.
cards.quote: in marmoset fetuses (Heide et al., Science, 2020), where it enlarged the neocortex and increased upper-layer neurons.
cards.section: Genes that only humans have

cards.front: How does NOTCH2NL connect gene duplication to prolonged cortical progenitor maintenance?
cards.back: It raises Notch signalling, which holds progenitors back from making neurons. Its functional copies derive from part of NOTCH2 and are human-specific.
cards.quote: NOTCH2NL raises Notch signalling, the signal that holds progenitors back from making neurons.
cards.section: Genes that only humans have

cards.front: NOTCH2NL expression in embryonic mouse cortex kept progenitors dividing. What opposite differentiation effect would its removal predict in human cortical organoids, and was it observed?
cards.back: Earlier differentiation into neurons. Deleting NOTCH2NL from human stem cells produced cortical organoids with early progenitor differentiation, consistent with losing a signal that delays neuron production.
cards.quote: found that deleting them from human stem cells made cortical organoids whose progenitors differentiated early.
cards.section: Genes that only humans have

cards.front: A gene perturbation leaves more neural progenitors at an endpoint. Why does that fail to establish increased symmetric proliferative division?
cards.back: More progenitors could reflect extra progenitor generation or slower differentiation. By the stated rule, symmetric amplification specifically requires both daughters to remain progenitors; pool size alone does not reveal division mode.
cards.quote: keeping a pool going is not the same as growing it.
cards.section: Genes that only humans have

cards.front: What neurogenesis durations are compared for mouse, rhesus monkey, and human cortex?
cards.back: About a week in mouse, roughly two months in rhesus monkey, and longer still in humans.
cards.quote: Cortical neurogenesis takes about a week in the mouse and roughly two months in the rhesus monkey
cards.section: Taking longer: development on a slower clock

cards.front: A neurogenic period becomes twice as long, but every cell cycle also becomes twice as long. With division modes and survival unchanged, does extra time guarantee more neurons?
cards.back: No. The number of available division rounds stays the same, so longer elapsed time alone does not increase output under these assumptions.
cards.quote: How many neurons that adds also depends on cell-cycle length and on the kind of division.
cards.section: Taking longer: development on a slower clock

cards.front: With unchanged cell-cycle length, why does extending neurogenesis have different effects on steady versus expanding progenitor pools?
cards.back: A steady pool adds neurons in proportion to time. An expanding pool creates more future neuron-producing cells, so extra time compounds output.
cards.quote: a pool that holds steady adds neurons in proportion to the time, and a pool that keeps growing compounds the extra time.
cards.section: Taking longer: development on a slower clock

cards.front: Retention of juvenile features for longer is called {{c1::neoteny}}.
cards.quote: Keeping juvenile features for longer is called neoteny.
cards.section: Outside the rule: how fast neurons mature

cards.front: How do human prefrontal synapse and spine observations qualify the idea of a single cortical maturation schedule?
cards.back: Prefrontal synaptic density peaks and declines later than auditory density; prefrontal pyramidal spine density remains above adult levels into the third decade. Timing varies by region and measure.
cards.quote: synaptic density in prefrontal cortex peaks later, and declines later, than in auditory cortex
cards.section: Outside the rule: how fast neurons mature

cards.front: SRGAP2C expression slows dendritic spine maturation and increases adult spine density in mouse cortical neurons. Does this demonstrate increased cortical neuron production?
cards.back: No. SRGAP2C acts on neurons, blocking the ancestral protein and altering spine maturation. Those measurements concern connections, not progenitor output or total neuron number.
cards.quote: Expressed in mouse cortical neurons, it slowed the maturation of dendritic spines and increased their density in the adult.
cards.section: Outside the rule: how fast neurons mature

cards.front: Human stem-cell-derived cortical neurons mature over months after transplantation into newborn mouse cortex, while neighbouring mouse neurons mature earlier. Which timing explanation is supported, and what remains unresolved?
cards.back: Part of the pace travels with the human cells, rather than being set wholly by the host. The shared environment comparison supports an intrinsic contribution but does not reveal how the cells encode their pace.
cards.quote: At least part of the timing travels with the human cells.
cards.section: Outside the rule: how fast neurons mature

cards.front: A perturbation delays spine maturation without changing measured neuron totals. Why would this be insufficient evidence for an enlarged progenitor pool?
cards.back: The stated rules separate connection maturation from neuron production. Delayed spine maturation describes neurons already made; evidence for progenitor amplification must address progenitors and their divisions, not maturation alone.
cards.quote: The slow maturation of synapses is a separate story.
cards.section: Putting it together

cards.front: How would you test whether outer radial glial doubling, rather than incoming progenitors or altered loss, expands a cortical progenitor pool?
cards.back: Film lineages in cortical slices and follow both daughters through later divisions, distinguishing radial glia from intermediate progenitors. Measure cycle length and loss. The stated rule identifies doubling by two persistent progenitor daughters; endpoint counts also reflect arrivals and departures.
cards.quote: new outer radial glia can arrive from the ventricular zone, and doubling can be balanced by cells that stop dividing or die.
cards.section: Design problem: a longer clock and a little doubling

cards.front: A toy lineage starts with one progenitor and no loss. Compare 60 with 120 rounds: either every division adds one neuron, or each progenitor doubles with probability 0.1 and otherwise adds one neuron. How does extending time affect output?
cards.back: Adding only: 120/60 = 2-fold. With doubling: N(t) = 9(1.1^t − 1); N(60) ≈ 2,731 and N(120) ≈ 834,373, about 305.5-fold. This follows the stated compounding rule; these are toy expectations, not species measurements.
cards.quote: roughly 300 times more, because the extra time compounds the doubling.
cards.section: Design problem: a longer clock and a little doubling

cards.front: How did the isotropic fractionator study distinguish neurons in dissolved human brain regions?
cards.back: It counted nuclei stained for NeuN, a protein found in neuronal nuclei, after making a suspension of cell nuclei.
cards.quote: dissolved each brain region into a suspension of cell nuclei, and counted the nuclei stained for NeuN
cards.section: How the 86 billion was counted

cards.front: Why is cerebral cortical mass a poor guide to which human brain region contains the most neurons?
cards.back: The cortex makes up most brain mass, but the cerebellum contains about 69 billion neurons, more than four times the cortical count in the cited study.
cards.quote: About 69 billion are in the cerebellum, more than four times as many as in the cerebral cortex
cards.section: How the 86 billion was counted

cards.front: A neuron-count study samples only four adult men. What limits should accompany an attempt to generalize its mean to all humans?
cards.back: The sample does not establish counts for women or children or characterize all population variation. The stated sampling limit and observed spread mean its mean should not be treated as a universal individual count.
cards.quote: So the figure has a real spread, and it says nothing yet about women, children or variation across people.
cards.section: How the 86 billion was counted

cards.front: How did the human-versus-chimpanzee HARE5 comparison in transgenic mice show that regulatory DNA can affect brain growth?
cards.back: The human enhancer version sped the progenitor cell cycle and enlarged the brain relative to the chimpanzee version. The experiment altered an enhancer of FZD8, not its protein-coding sequence.
cards.quote: The human version of HARE5, an enhancer of the Wnt receptor gene FZD8, sped up the progenitor cell cycle
cards.section: Other candidate genes and regulatory changes
